notes: Only slots 8-12 written, as catchy German labels matching the authored DDR set. All five are small circles of Arab and Iranian students and diplomats in the GDR (recognized by Iraq, Sudan, Syria, South Yemen and Egypt in 1969), tied to real West German and Middle Eastern institutions: Islamic Centre Hamburg, Najaf/Dawa, Hizb ut-Tahrir, Said Ramadan's Munich mosque circle. No invented persons.

8.name: Der Draht nach Hamburg
8.text:
Der Draht nach Hamburg is a small circle of Shia students from Iraq, Lebanon and Iran at the universities of East Berlin, Leipzig and Dresden who keep in touch, through trips across the Friedrichstraße crossing, with the Islamic Centre Hamburg and its Imam Ali Mosque on the Alster, the leading Shia institution in Western Europe. Many of them first met at Leipzig's Herder Institute, where foreign students learn German.

The circle favours a modern, socially engaged Shia Islam that answers Marxism with its own vision of justice, as taught by the reformist clerics of Hamburg and Qom. It seeks dialogue rather than confrontation with the socialist state. Its members are few and watched by the Stasi, but they are the future engineers, doctors and officials of their home countries.

9.name: Der Kerbela-Kreis
9.text:
Der Kerbela-Kreis is a handful of Iraqi Shia students sent to the GDR by Baghdad's Ba'athist government who secretly follow the clergy of Najaf and the Islamic Dawa movement inspired by Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr. They meet for prayer and the Muharram mourning of Imam Husayn in dormitory rooms in Leipzig, Dresden and Freiberg, out of sight of both the Iraqi embassy and the Stasi.

They regard Ba'athism and communism alike as godless tyranny and dream of an Islamic order led by the senior clergy, beginning with the fall of the Ba'ath in Baghdad. They see the GDR, Baghdad's new partner, as an accomplice of their persecutors. Their influence inside the Republic is nil, but every contact they make is a potential embarrassment for East Berlin's Arab diplomacy.

10.name: Die Pankower Gebetsstube
10.text:
Die Pankower Gebetsstube is the prayer room kept by the Arab missions in East Berlin, whose diplomats arrived after Iraq, Sudan, Syria, South Yemen and Egypt recognized the GDR in 1969. On Fridays it gathers diplomats, trade officials, students and the capital's few Muslims, under the eye of the Foreign Ministry, which values every gesture of respect toward its new partners.

The prayers are led by embassy staff who preach an orthodox, apolitical Islam loyal to the governments that sent them and to the religious establishment of al-Azhar. They avoid any criticism of the socialist state and welcome its support for the Arab cause against Israel. Their leverage is diplomatic: for a republic hungry for recognition, the goodwill of the Arab world is worth a prayer room or two.

11.name: Die Kalifatszelle
11.text:
Die Kalifatszelle is a tiny network of Palestinian, Jordanian and Syrian students at the universities of Leipzig, Halle and Dresden who follow Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani. They pass its pamphlets from hand to hand and recruit quietly among Muslim students in the dormitories, keeping their links to the party's members in West Berlin.

The cell teaches that neither socialism nor nationalism can free the Muslims, only a restored caliphate ruling by the sharia, and it regards the Arab regimes befriending the GDR as apostates. It rejects every form of cooperation with the atheist state. It has no recognized leader and no hope of a German following, but the Stasi takes its contacts with the West and the Middle East seriously.

12.name: Die stillen Brüder
12.text:
Die stillen Brüder are Egyptian, Syrian and Sudanese students and trainees in the GDR who sympathize with the Muslim Brotherhood, banned and persecuted by Nasser's Egypt and the Ba'ath in Damascus. Through relatives and visits to West Berlin they keep contact with the Brotherhood's exile network in West Germany, centred on the Munich mosque circle founded by Said Ramadan and on Syrian exiles in Aachen.

They seek an Islamic society of moral renewal, social justice and consultation, opposing both the materialism of the East and the decadence of the West, and they reject the secular nationalist regimes that sent them abroad. Their method is patience: study hard, keep the faith, avoid open politics. Their numbers are small, but they form a disciplined core among the Republic's Arab students.
